subject: Broadcom sells the chips and arranges the loans
bodyMarkdown:
Broadcom has spent the past week lining up tens of billions of dollars in loans so that OpenAI and Anthropic can buy chips from Broadcom. If you hold a broad index fund, you own a slice of that arrangement, and it is worth knowing how it is put together.

## Broadcom became the lender too

Bloomberg reported on Thursday that Broadcom is in early talks to arrange debt financing for OpenAI's custom chips, with discussions pointing to roughly $30 billion for the next phase of the project. The Wall Street Journal put the figure above $50 billion. Both reports stress that the talks are early, that private credit firms including Apollo Global Management and Blackstone are involved, and that nothing is expected to be signed before the end of the year. The size is a range right now, not a number.

The Anthropic version is further along. Bloomberg reported on October 2 that Broadcom's bank syndicate is assembling about $60 billion, split into a $42 billion senior secured tranche being marketed by Bank of America, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley, and an $18 billion junior tranche led by Blackstone, which is committing $9 billion of its own capital.

## Why the lenders wanted a backstop

Here is the part I keep turning over. Broadcom is not only selling the chips and introducing the lenders. On the Anthropic deal, Bloomberg reported that Broadcom is providing **residual value support**, meaning Broadcom absorbs part of the loss if the hardware turns out to be worth less than projected when the loan comes due. Broadcom carries an A-minus credit rating, so that promise is worth something real. It also means a single company is the supplier, the arranger and the guarantor of the collateral.

The lenders asked for it because nobody knows what a three-year-old AI accelerator is worth. That is the whole question. Most of this money is **private credit**, lending by investment funds rather than by banks, which prices in private and reports slowly. The Bank for International Settlements made the point in a bulletin this year that leverage parked in a separate vehicle is still leverage.

## What a Canadian reader does with this

Probably nothing, and I would rather say so than invent an action. Your exposure runs through index funds and pension plans, not through anything you sign at a branch. The reason to follow it anyway is that this is the first stretch of the AI buildout being paid for mostly with borrowed money instead of cash flow, and borrowed money has a price that other people set. The federal funds range sits at 3.75 to 4 per cent. DisruptionBanking reported in late September that AI-linked corporate bonds were trading about 1.15 percentage points above government bonds, against 0.78 for investment grade broadly, while cautioning that those are different groups of borrowers.

## The takeaway

Watch whether these loans actually price, and at what spread, because that will tell you more about the pace of the buildout than any model launch does. The Anthropic syndication is in the market now, so a real answer arrives within weeks rather than quarters. If the senior tranche clears near par and that spread gap holds near where it sat in late September, the buildout keeps its current speed. If the gap widens while Broadcom is still carrying the residual value risk, then the binding constraint on AI becomes credit rather than silicon.
